data.title: Meduza: The Russian-born collaboration platform Miro has a new owner. Meet Bending Spoons, the tech giant that buys popular apps, cuts jobs, and raises prices.
data.summary: In late October, Miro — a collaboration platform created by Russian developers that took off during the pandemic — got a new owner. The buyer was Bending Spoons, an Italian technology company that acquires well-known internet projects past their peak of popularity. Bending Spoons’s tactic is simple: buy a business with a strong customer base, cut the team, and raise prices, using the resulting profit growth to fund the purchase of a new business. Investors like this model: Bending Spoons is growing aggressively on borrowed money, and its shareholders even include Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway conglomerate. Users of the services the Italian company buys up, however, are far less pleased.

data.title: Meduza: She moved from Russia to Germany to work as a nanny. She ended up founding a learning center for Russian-speaking children — and winning over skeptical local officials.
data.summary: The new subject of our “Emigrant Questionnaire” column is Alexandra Konopleva, who has lived in Germany for almost 14 years now. In Russia, Alexandra worked in a kindergarten, a school, and summer camps, and she moved to Germany as a nanny under the Au Pair program. Here she completed a master’s degree (even though she couldn’t understand what people were saying to her during her entrance exams) and founded an educational center for Russian-speaking children called Chemodan Skazok (“Suitcase of Fairy Tales”). She also became a volunteer firefighter, made a documentary film, and joined her city council.

The investigative outlet iStories highlighted the figure after reviewing a database of Russian front-line military losses compiled by Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency, and shared by hackers. Meduza and other news outlets reviewed the same data at the same time.

data.title: Meduza: More than 700,000 Russian troops died in the war in Ukraine by late September 2026, Meduza and Mediazona estimate
data.summary: On November 1, news broke that hackers from the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow had breached the website of Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency, and obtained data on Russian military losses in the war through fall 2026. The hackers used that data to produce their own estimate of how many Russians had been killed on the front lines. They also shared the database with reporters, including those at Meduza and Mediazona, which have been tracking Russia’s military death toll together for several years. We examined the hacked database and concluded that it was very likely authentic. We then compared its records with other sources and ran a new analysis. Our earlier studies relied mainly on data from the Register of Inheritance Cases. The Rosstat database makes the new estimate more reliable. Another important change: The new estimate counts both registered deaths and missing service members, many of whom will likely be confirmed dead.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/11/23/.label: Meduza: More than 700,000 Russian troops died in the war in Ukraine by late September 2026, Meduza and Mediazona estimate
